why: A battery whose stored chemicals cost about a dollar per kilowatt-hour would make holding a whole season of power affordable, and nobody is building the sulfur-air version.
found: Form Energy began on this MIT chemistry and pivoted to iron-air; Imperial's polysulfide-air spin-out RFC Power is now Certain Energy, commercialising manganese flow batteries instead; nothing deployed.

why: Running one ceramic cell both ways between a methane cavern and a CO2 cavern would let existing gas caverns hold months of power at about 70% round trip.
found: Only the 2015 DTU/Stanford design study, a School of Mines model and a completed DOE lab project on reversible methane cells; no company or cavern pilot.

why: Found Energy already runs aluminium-water reactors that give hydrogen and heat and send the oxide back for re-smelting, so the question is whether using that loop seasonally, with summer power doing the smelting, is a new device. My pick: drop.
found: Found Energy (Boston) runs a 100 kW-class aluminium-water demo plant making heat and hydrogen from treated scrap, with spent oxide recyclable to metal; seasonal use only in Swiss/EU research (SPF HybridStock, REVEAL).

why: Saving desert sunshine as heaps of sulfur that keep for years would let solar plants sell summer power in winter, at a capacity cost hundreds of times below batteries.
found: Only the EU PEGASUS research project (DLR, 2016-2021) with a 500 kWth particle receiver and sulfur burner tests; no commercial plant or company.

why: Deep Fission is already building exactly this, a reactor in a mile-deep borehole with water pressure doing the vessel's job, at Parsons, Kansas.
found: Deep Fission broke ground in December 2025 on a 15 MWe borehole reactor under the DOE reactor pilot programme.

why: Helion Energy is already building this machine, a pulsed magnetic-compression fusion plant that recovers electricity directly with no steam, for Microsoft.
found: Helion broke ground on its 50 MW Orion plant in Malaga, Washington in July 2025 and secured state licences in June 2026; Polaris prototype operating since 2024.

why: Acceleron Fusion, with about $24M raised, is already designing a muon-catalysed fusion power plant, and the physics is still below breakeven.
found: Acceleron Fusion (Lowercarbon-backed, ARPA-E grants) is designing a muon-catalysed fusion plant and plans a breakeven test at Brookhaven; Marathon Fusion also works on it.

why: Funded startups are already drilling wells that pump water into iron-rich rock to make hydrogen, so this is being built.
found: Vema Hydrogen drilled pilot wells in Quebec and plans a commercial well; GeoRedox and Canada Nickel launched a stimulated hydrogen well in Ontario; Eden GeoPower and others have ARPA-E-funded pilots.

why: Verdox, the funded MIT spin-out, holds a DOE award to build exactly this electro-swing electrode capture for air, and several electric DAC startups already run pilots.
found: Verdox (Breakthrough Energy-backed) has a DOE project 'Electro-swing adsorption for high efficiency direct air capture'; Phlair, Ucaneo and RepAir run electrochemical capture pilots.

why: Letting sunlight itself release captured CO2 removes the heat bill that is most of air capture's cost; only ORNL lab cycles exist, though the light used so far is ultraviolet.
found: Only ORNL lab work (metastable photoacid, Angewandte 2023; photobase photo-DAC, JACS 2026); Holocene licensed a different ORNL sorbent and was bought by Occidental; no light-driven pilot.

why: Surface seawater holds only about 90 grams of CO2 per cubic metre, so a gigaton a year means pushing roughly ten thousand cubic kilometres of water through tight rock; can any well field move that much? My pick: drop.
found: 44.01 mineralises already-captured CO2 dissolved in seawater in Oman and UAE peridotite (Series A $37M); nobody circulates plain seawater to draw CO2 from the air.

why: Small solar-powered reverse-osmosis units already give families drinking water from brackish ground off-grid, so is a still that needs no pump or membrane a 10x change or just a better still? My pick: drop.
found: Only MIT/Shanghai Jiao Tong lab and rooftop prototypes (EES 2020) and research variants; no commercial multistage passive still found.

why: The effect it rests on is in doubt: a 2026 Max Planck PNAS study found visible light at solar intensity does not measurably speed evaporation.
found: MIT photomolecular-effect papers (PNAS 2023, 2024) only; Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research replication in PNAS 2026 found no effect.

why: For a family's drinking water from brackish ground, small solar reverse-osmosis units already work off-grid, and this method's real strength is very salty industrial brine while it leaves traces of amine solvent in the water.
found: Columbia (Yip lab) TSSE papers and patents only; no spin-out, pilot or field unit.

why: Nobody sells a cheap whole-body screening scanner, but can a 0.05 T image cleaned up by a model trained on strong-magnet scans show a few-millimetre stage-1 tumour without inventing or erasing detail? My pick: keep.
found: HKU 0.05 T whole-body scanner (Science 2024) is a research prototype with no spin-off found; Hyperfine Swoop is head-only; low-field breast MRI is a 14-person study; whole-body screening (Prenuvo, Ezra) uses costly standard MRI.

why: A swallowed probiotic that multiplies only inside tumours turns a millimetre growth into a urine signal on a paper strip, a cheap screen for cancers far smaller than blood tests can see.
found: Only mouse studies (Danino, MIT 2015; Columbia/Adelaide colorectal 2024) and a human trial of unengineered E. coli Nissle colonising tumours; MIT lists the tech for licensing; no company or diagnostic trial.

why: A wire slipped into an arm vein to catch tumour cells already exists as the CE-marked GILUPI CellCollector, so magnets on the wire are a better catch for the same device and patients.
found: GILUPI CellCollector, an antibody-coated wire left 30 minutes in a vein, used in prostate and colorectal cancer studies; MagWIRE (Stanford) is its magnetic successor, tested in pigs.

why: It watches for spread in people already treated for cancer, so it doesn't make routine, cheap stage-1 detection possible for everyone else.
found: Michigan/Northwestern mouse studies only; a human protocol for post-treatment breast cancer monitoring proposed since 2016; no registered trial found.
